evidence: This claim is supported by the broader literature and examples provided throughout the manuscript.

claim: Consumers break down some DLs into basic molecules (e.g., free fatty acids) but not others (sterols).

claim: Biotechnological yeast production increases manifold when only parts of sterol production pathways are switched off.
source: The growth and fitness benefits of switching off the sterol-producing machinery are very large: biotechnological yeast production (i.e., offspring number, or fitness) increases manifold even when only parts of sterol production pathways are switched off (e.g., Johnston et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Johnston et al., 2020.

claim: If using dietary sterols allowed abandoning the sterol production in nature and resources for defence and reproduction were freed, extinction risks may have been generally reduced but especially so in changing temperatures.
source: If using dietary sterols allowed abandoning the sterol production in nature and resources for defence and reproduction were freed, extinction risks may have been generally reduced but especially so in changing temperatures.
evidence: This is speculation about evolutionary consequences.

claim: Sterol auxotrophy likely was a cheaper option than producing multiple sterol production pathways to resist different temperatures, whereby sterols were taken up in response to temperature.
source: The large costs of sterol production make it also unlikely that multiple sterol production pathways have evolved that equipped membranes with different sterols to resist different temperatures. Sterol auxotrophy likely was the much cheaper option whereby sterols were taken up in response to temperature (Brankatschk et al., 2018; Knittelfelder et al., 2020).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations.

claim: Sterol independence would have allowed insects and nematodes to colonise low-oxygen but sterol-rich environments, such as soil and rotting organic material.
source: Sterol independence would, in turn, have allowed insects and nematodes to colonise low-oxygen but sterol-rich environments, such as soil and rotting organic material.
evidence: This is speculation about ecological consequences of sterol auxotrophy.

claim: While arthropods and nematodes form the clade Ecdysozoa, sterol auxotrophy may have evolved independently in both groups.
source: For example, while arthropods and nematodes form the clade Ecdysozoa, sterol auxotrophy may have evolved independently in both groups.
evidence: This is speculation about evolutionary history.

claim: Species-poor related sister clades, such as the tardigrades or the Scalidophora, retain the full set of cholesterol-producing genes.
source: This idea would be consistent with the retention of the full set of cholesterol-producing genes (Zhang et al., 2019) in species-poor related sister clades, such as the tardigrades or, depending on the phylogenetic hypothesis (Dunn et al., 2014), the Scalidophora.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2019 and Dunn et al., 2014.

claim: There are some non-ecdysozoan taxa that have lost cholesterol-producing genes but their ability to produce other sterols is unknown.
source: On the other hand, there are some non-ecdysozoan taxa that have lost cholesterol-producing genes (Zhang et al., 2019) but their ability to produce other sterols is unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2019.

claim: Most lipid cell biology research is based on few cell lines derived from the muscle tissue of only a few individuals.
source: Much of current lipid cell biology research is based on few cell lines derived from the muscle tissue of only a few individuals (Pradas et al., 2018), and most experiments are carried out at 37°C, the core body temperature of most mammals.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pradas et al., 2018.

claim: Most lipid cell biology experiments are carried out at 37°C, the core body temperature of most mammals.

claim: The legs of birds are up to 10°C cooler than the body core temperature for long periods of time.
source: For example, the legs of birds (Steen and Steen, 2018) or toes and digits of humans are up to 10°C cooler than the body core temperature for long periods of time.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Steen and Steen, 2018.

source: For example, the legs of birds (Steen and Steen, 2018) or toes and digits of humans are up to 10°C cooler than the body core temperature for long periods of time.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about human physiology.

claim: The sperm of birds and mammals largely and consistently differ in FA composition.
source: The sperm of birds and mammals largely and consistently also differ in FA composition (Surai et al., 2007) and temperature.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Surai et al., 2007.

claim: In the external scrotum of mammals, sperm are up to 8 degrees below body temperature (~30°C) whereas in birds sperm are at body temperature (~40°C).
source: In the external scrotum of mammals, sperm are up to 8° degrees below body temperature (~30°C) whereas in birds sperm are at body temperature (~40°C).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about reproductive physiology.

claim: DLs affect the neuronal lipid profile in insects.
source: DLs affect the neuronal lipid profile in insects (Carvalho et al., 2012), and are essential for the normal development and function of the central nervous system in vertebrates (Cole et al., 2010; González et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Carvalho et al., 2012.

claim: DLs are essential for the normal development and function of the central nervous system in vertebrates.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cole et al., 2010 and González et al., 2010.

claim: Experimentally decreasing the saturation of FA in the neurons leads to what is observed after consuming plant lipids: individuals predictably choose lower temperatures in D. melanogaster.
source: New evidence shows that the saturation of FAs determines neuronal function in D. melanogaster: Experimentally decreasing the saturation of FA in the neurons leads to what is observed after consuming plant lipids: individuals predictably choose lower temperatures (Suito et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Suito et al., 2020.

claim: Alterations of the brain lipidome are hallmarks of neurodegenerative diseases and neuronal aging.
source: As alterations of the brain lipidome are hallmarks of neurodegenerative diseases and neuronal aging (Huynh et al., 2020), DL interventions may have a yet undisclosed therapeutic potential.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Huynh et al., 2020.

claim: DL interventions may have a yet undisclosed therapeutic potential for neurodegenerative diseases and neuronal aging.

claim: Many pathways of lipid processing are molecularly or functionally conserved across the animal kingdom, such as the lipoprotein system, LDL receptors, desaturases, or lipases.
source: Many pathways of lipid processing are molecularly or functionally conserved across the animal kingdom, such as the lipoprotein system, LDL receptors, desaturases, or lipases.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about lipid metabolism.

claim: Drosophila and Caenorhabditis elegans represent potent models to assess health impacts, metabolic malfunction, and other organismal consequences of lipid function in cell membranes.
source: Therefore, Drosophila (sterol and PUFA auxotroph) and Caenorhabditis elegans (sterol auxotroph) represent potent models to assess health impacts, metabolic malfunction, and other organismal consequences of lipid function in cell membranes.
evidence: This is an inference about the utility of model organisms.

claim: Biomedical research on the genetic causes of diseases that affect lipid metabolism may help to explain selection pressures that shape intraspecific genetic variation for lipid processing enzymes in the wild or even lipid selectivity.
source: In reverse, biomedical research on the genetic causes of diseases that affect lipid metabolism may help to explain selection pressures that shape intraspecific genetic variation for lipid processing enzymes in the wild (Twining et al., 2021) or even lipid selectivity.
evidence: This is speculation about the bidirectional benefits of research.
